title: Islamic Greetings
summary: The meaning behind "as-salamu alaykum" and a handful of other common Arabic phrases you'll hear constantly.

body.text: "Peace be upon you" is a prayer, not just hello

As-salamu alaykum ("peace be upon you") is the standard Islamic greeting, and it's treated as more than a formality — it's literally a short prayer for the other person's wellbeing. The typical reply is wa alaykumu s-salam ("and upon you be peace"), and it's considered good practice to reply with an equal or slightly longer greeting than the one you received.

body.translation: You will not enter Paradise until you believe, and you will not believe until you love one another. Shall I not guide you to something which, if you do, you will love one another? Spread salaam among yourselves.

body.text: This hadith is often quoted specifically because it ties something as small as a greeting to something as big as building real community — the idea is that a habit of greeting people warmly and often is part of what builds the trust and closeness the hadith is describing.
A handful of other everyday phrases

You'll hear these constantly in Muslim company, and picking them up early makes conversations feel far less foreign:

• Bismillah — "in the name of Allah," said before starting almost anything (eating, a task, a journey).
• Alhamdulillah — "praise be to Allah," said in response to good news, or simply as a general expression of gratitude, including in answer to "how are you?"
• InshaAllah — "if Allah wills," said when talking about future plans, as a small reminder that outcomes ultimately aren't fully in our own hands.
• MashaAllah — "what Allah has willed," said when admiring something good (a person's success, a baby, a nice house) — often paired with a prayer against envy.
• SubhanAllah — "glory be to Allah," an expression of amazement, often at something beautiful or impressive in creation.
• JazakAllahu khairan — "may Allah reward you with good," a common way of saying thank you.

body.question: Can I say "as-salamu alaykum" to someone who isn't Muslim?
body.answer: Yes — many Muslims do use it broadly as a friendly greeting, though some choose a more neutral greeting with people they know aren't Muslim, based on differing scholarly views on the specific etiquette involved. Either approach is common in practice; it's a matter of personal comfort, not a strict rule you need to worry over.

body.question: Do I have to use these phrases perfectly and immediately?
body.answer: Not at all. Nobody expects a new Muslim to have flawless pronunciation from day one — these phrases are picked up gradually through hearing and using them, the same way anyone learns the natural rhythms of a new language. Using a phrase imperfectly and being corrected kindly is a completely normal part of the process.

body.question: Pick one phrase from this lesson to try using today, even if just in your own head or with a Muslim friend. Which one felt most natural to start with?
